name: Aaron Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aaron, forty-three, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I wire homes and repair shop electrics for a small contractor, mostly the ordinary jobs rather than the really complicated faults. I like leaving a customer able to use the kitchen again; I don't like finding another visit added to the phone before I've finished the first.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening around work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Tessa packs orders for a catering firm, and our children are eight and eleven. We have a mortgage, three weeks of expenses saved and my lower-than-usual electrician's pay, with only a few similar firms nearby. I use AI occasionally to draft a customer explanation, once a colleague has checked the tool, and I compare it with my actual test sheet before sending anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say useful tools can stay without everyone making a grand speech. I'd rather the firm gave us a proper paid day than another subscription nobody asked for. I'd bring the low wage up through our union rep. A faster customer message isn't money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the household money already. Tessa and I cover the bills together, but three weeks saved wouldn't hold the mortgage very long if either wage stopped. I've been doing this long enough to know the work; that doesn't mean there is another employer down the road offering better pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the same wiring and repair shifts now and throughout the first year. I'd continue checking occasional AI drafts against my own test sheets, and ask the union rep next month to pursue the overdue pay review. We'd cancel our two monthly cinema visits and use the money towards current bills instead of pretending it pays for a new qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, with some relief that the work stays recognisable. I don't need excitement to enjoy fixing something, but I would like to stop checking the balance before buying school shoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the pay review to use as evidence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The actual jobs we complete, the hours we work and what the owner has already promised in writing. I'd rather the rep took a clear request than a pile of rumours about what other firms pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would replace the cinema trips?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A film at home after the children go to bed, assuming we're both awake. The saving is small, but those are tickets we haven't bought; it isn't a promise to cut the mortgage payment.

say: I'd keep **useful small tools** without treating every new subscription as a change in the world.
I'd ask the union rep to pursue **better pay**, because a quicker message is not money in the bank.
think: I'm already **anxious about money**, with both wages needed and only three weeks saved.
My **electrical experience** does not create better-paid nearby vacancies where there are few other employers.
do: Keep **wiring and repair shifts** and check occasional AI drafts against actual test sheets.
Ask the **union rep** next month to pursue the overdue pay review using written promises and actual hours.
Cancel **two monthly cinema visits** and use the money for current household bills.
feel: **Anxious about bills**, while relieved that the familiar work remains useful.
S0.quote: A faster customer message isn't money in the bank.
fieldNote: His **experience and licence** allow ordinary independent work, while low pay and few employers keep the household budget fragile.
The **cinema cut** frees money for existing bills, with neither a course fund nor new savings claimed from the same small amount.

steps.text: Keep wiring and repair shifts on the present rota
Ask the union rep to pursue the overdue pay review next month
Cancel two monthly cinema visits to help cover current bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's measure what gets quicker and agree where the saved hours go. I'd ask the union rep to seek paid tool practice and a limit on added visits. I don't want the crew correcting bad quotes in our own time because somebody already sold the saving to a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours could shrink if the firm wins work by quoting fewer paid hours for each repair. Most of the job is still physical, so I don't expect the whole trade to disappear in this picture. I worry more about being paid for a shorter day while somehow still finishing the same number of houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take part in a four-week paid quoting trial only after our estimator checks it on finished jobs. I'd write down actual visit and travel times, then take the comparison to the union rep during the first year. At home we'd keep the cinema cut and delay the planned new dining table until we know whether the paid hours change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a bit of interest in the trial. I can see the point of a useful tool, but I want the wage agreement before anyone celebrates the saved time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write down if the quote was wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The task missing from the allowance and the actual time it took, without putting the customer's name into a public document. A hidden damaged cable doesn't disappear because the plan didn't include it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask the union rather than make your own arrangement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if one person accepts unpaid checking, the next person gets told it's normal. I'd rather the whole crew has a clear paid rule, including the quieter people who don't argue much.

say: I'd ask the union to agree **saved hours** before they become extra visits or unpaid checking.
I'd want **paid practice** and actual measurements before the firm celebrates a quicker quote.
think: My **paid hours could shrink** if cheaper quotes squeeze the time allowed for real repairs.
I expect **physical work to continue**, but worry about fitting the same houses into a smaller paid day.
do: Join a **four-week paid trial** only after the estimator checks the quoting tool on finished jobs.
Record **visit and travel times** and take the comparison to the union rep during the first year.
Keep the **cinema cut** and delay the uncommitted dining-table purchase while paid hours remain uncertain.
feel: **Anxious but interested**, wanting a wage agreement before celebrating time saved.
S1.quote: A hidden damaged cable doesn't disappear because the plan didn't include it.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **physical demand** from paid time allowed, recognising a route to lower earnings without claiming thinking software performs a repair.
His **collective request** protects paid checking across the crew rather than relying on a personal exception that others may not receive.

steps.text: Trial the quoting tool for four paid weeks after estimator checks
Take actual visit and travel times to the union to seek paid checking
Keep cinema cuts and delay the uncommitted dining-table purchase

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning changes in 2028 and the robots follow around 2031, so we need an agreement covering both. I'd ask the union to seek written notice, paid training and a real income bridge if hours are cut. I'd rather have the eligibility rules on paper than a speech telling working families to be resilient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to lose a big part of my repair hours once robots can do the physical jobs around 2031, even if some awkward work remains. My firm might lose customers to contractors able to buy the machines, and Tessa's packing work could face robots too. At forty-eight, with children and a mortgage, I can't make three weeks of savings stand in for a second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union adviser which hardship help exists, what qualifies and whether any payment is a loan. Tessa and I would ask the mortgage lender about temporary options and total costs before agreeing to anything. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for advertised equipment-service posts only if they include paid practical learning and written wages after travel that cover our bills, keeping this job until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, especially at night when I start adding up months instead of weeks. I can make enquiries, but I don't yet have a paid route that covers what the family needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would equipment service be safe from the same robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not guaranteed, no. I'd ask what paid work actually exists and learn something useful while there is work, rather than call a different job title permanent shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you refuse from a hardship offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything presented as free help when it's really debt with costs nobody has explained. I'd want the repayment and eligibility terms before putting even one payment into our budget.

say: I'd ask for **written notice and training** that cover planning changes in 2028 and robots around 2031.
I'd want **income-bridge eligibility** on paper rather than a speech about resilience.
think: I expect **a big repair-hours loss** when robots arrive around 2031, despite some difficult physical work remaining.
Tessa's **packing income** could also face robots, leaving three weeks saved against a mortgage and children.
do: Ask the **union adviser** now about hardship help, eligibility and whether payments are loans.
Ask the lender about **temporary mortgage options** and total costs before agreeing.
Apply after 2028 for **advertised service posts** only with paid learning and affordable written wages after travel.
feel: **Alarmed at night**, expecting a major hours loss without a funded household route yet.
S2.quote: I don't yet have a paid route that covers what the family needs.
fieldNote: His **expected physical-work loss** follows robots around 2031, while earlier planning changes and later service work offer no permanent shelter.
He checks **support and loan terms** before counting money, and another post must provide paid learning with a signed affordable wage.

steps.text: Ask the union adviser about hardship eligibility and possible repayment terms
Ask the lender about temporary mortgage options and total costs
Apply after 2028 to advertised service jobs with paid learning and wages covering bills after travel
Keep current job until a suitable written offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us test a proper paid route instead of promising everybody will somehow adapt. I'd ask the union to negotiate training places that state the wage, teaching time and real task afterwards. A course link is not an agreement to pay someone while learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income could still fall, but I have more time to investigate a practical skill route before the planning changes in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one, so retirement isn't a plan I can assume will arrive first. I'd rather learn from a proven class while keeping the wage than resign and hope a course produces a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask now for the next proven small class in building-control servicing, speaking to two earlier learners about what equipment they actually used. I'd enrol after 2031 only with employer-paid fees, my normal wage maintained and supervised paid practice afterwards. We'd keep the cinema cut and try saving twenty-five monthly only when all essential bills are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see a sequence of choices rather than one jump. Checking a class with people who've taken it sounds like me; buying the first promise out of fear doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the two learners report different things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the provider to show the workshop timetable and equipment, then wait until I could check the answer. I wouldn't pay the deposit to settle the argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if normal wages are kept but total hours are reduced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd need the full weekly pay protected before agreeing. The mortgage takes money for the week, not an impressive hourly rate for fewer hours.

say: I'd ask the union for **real paid places** rather than a general promise that workers will adapt.
I'd want **wage and teaching time** written down alongside the actual task after training.
think: My **income could fall**, but five years allows checking a skill route before planning changes in 2031.
At **fifty-one in 2034**, I cannot assume retirement arrives before physical robots change the work.
do: Check a **proven servicing class** with two earlier learners and verify equipment where accounts differ.
Take the **proven class** after 2031 only with employer-paid fees, full weekly pay protected and supervised paid practice afterwards.
Keep the **cinema cut** and save twenty-five monthly only after essential bills are paid.
feel: **Anxious but deliberate**, preferring a checked sequence of choices to a fearful leap.
S3.quote: The mortgage takes money for the week, not an impressive hourly rate for fewer hours.
fieldNote: His **steady adoption** favours a class tested by previous learners, with conflicting reports triggering a check rather than a hurried deposit.
He clarifies **full weekly pay** protection, ensuring that maintained hourly rates cannot hide lost paid hours during training.

steps.text: Take proven servicing after 2031 with employer-paid fees, protected full weekly pay and supervised paid practice
Keep cancelling two monthly cinema visits to cover current bills
Save twenty-five monthly only after essential bills are paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the children need room to see different kinds of work rather than hear one supposedly safe career at every dinner. I'd ask the school about free visits to workplaces they are curious about. I'd still support the union seeking paid adult classes, because a long warning is useful only if people can afford to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three weeks saved and low pay still make me anxious about this year's bills. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I'll be fifty-three, and robots around 2039 when I'll be fifty-six. The children will be eighteen and twenty-one at the thinking-AI date, but I don't know what they will earn or what mortgage balance we'll have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking about the proven servicing class now and save twenty-five monthly only after essentials are covered. This year I'd ask the school about free work visits in several fields the children choose. In the first year after 2036 I'd take the class only with paid fees, full weekly pay protected and supervised paid practice, not because the name sounds safer than my current job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the present and less rushed by the future. I'd like the children to see that preparing can mean checking a real offer, not spending every evening frightened by a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the extra years to buy robots yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without customers, prices and a maintenance bill I could afford, none of which I have now. My money already has a job paying household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the children ask whether they should leave school for a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what interests them and arrange a proper visit before changing any plan. I won't promise a lifetime of work in my trade just because I know how to do today's repairs.

say: I'd encourage **varied free work visits** rather than choose one supposedly safe career for the children.
I'd support **paid adult classes** because families need money as well as warning time to prepare.
think: Our **three-week reserve** and low pay keep this year's bills worrying despite the longer timetable.
I cannot assume **future child earnings** or a cleared mortgage when robots arrive around 2039.
do: Check the **proven servicing class** now and save twenty-five monthly only after essential bills.
Ask the school about **free work visits** across fields the children choose.
Take the **proven class** after 2036 only with employer-paid fees, full weekly pay protected and supervised paid practice afterwards.
feel: **Anxious about today**, but less rushed by future change and able to compare actual offers.
S4.quote: My money already has a job paying household bills.
fieldNote: His **children's ages** advance consistently, without their possible future wages or an assumed paid-off mortgage being used to close today's budget gap.
He rejects **speculative machine buying** because prices, customers and maintenance costs are unknown, keeping preparation tied to funded learning.

steps.text: Take proven servicing after 2036 with employer-paid fees, protected full weekly pay and supervised paid practice
Save twenty-five monthly only after essential bills are covered
Ask the school for free work visits across fields the children choose

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the planning changes start quickly and the robots could take much of our physical work around 2031. Paid practical training with the full weekly wage protected would help, along with clear temporary support if hours go. I'd want the union involved in checking the terms, especially for people with no spare month of money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a promised wage means after the hours have changed. A family can't eat an hourly rate. I want to know what reaches the bank at the end of the week, not just the number on a training poster.

headlineQuote: A family can't eat an hourly rate.
portrait: Aaron is a **43-year-old experienced electrician** with a vocational certificate and licence, doing ordinary house wiring and shop repairs.
He has **three weeks saved**, lower pay, few nearby employers, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with packing-worker wife Tessa.
He uses **AI occasionally** after colleague testing, favouring paid trials and proven classes over early adoption.
He is **already anxious** about bills, expects serious robot-related hours loss in the quick picture, and wants union-checked full weekly pay protection.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings quick planning changes before robots around 2031 could take much of the household's physical work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical training** should protect the full weekly wage as well as cover fees.
**Clear temporary support** and union checks of written terms would help if paid hours disappear.
